source.title: The Rate-Distortion-Polysemanticity Tradeoff in SAEs
source.authors: Tommaso Mencattini; Francesco Montagna; Francesco Locatello

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests polysemanticity mechanisms in toy SAEs and evaluates proxy measurements of SAE polysemanticity, using methods different from the cited neuron-level work.
record.gate_note: The synthetic SAE results and SAEBench proxy audit bear on the claim. The paper does not test vision neurons, transformer MLP neurons, or whether individual neurons have coherent jobs. Its proxy audit tests candidate SAE metrics against the paper's rate-distortion-polysemanticity criterion, not against known ground-truth polysemanticity in real models.
record.test_reason: The study measures polysemanticity of SAE dictionary atoms against a synthetic ground-truth DGP, not of neurons in trained vision or language models. That is a related but different construct (SAE latents, not network neurons), so it tests no version. Its only neuron-level content is a related-work mention of superposition. The proxy audit (Table 2) scores SAEBench interpretability metrics for SAEs against the paper's own theoretical RDP monotonicity criterion. It is not a test of how neuron polysemanticity is classified (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Under toy assumptions, optimal SAEs are polysemantic to exploit concept co-occurrence, and enforcing monosemanticity costs rate or distortion. The authors frame polysemanticity as a data problem: lowering it without cost needs changes to the training distribution, not just architecture or optimizer. Existing SAEBench proxies, AutoInterp especially, mostly fail their necessary RDP criterion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a formal toy DGP, synthetic SAE sweeps, and an audit of existing Gemma SAE proxy scores; it does not apply the original neuron-level visualization or intervention methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Synthetic toy results depend on the DGP co-occurrence probabilities and rate constraint; proxy-audit outcomes differ between TopK and ReLU SAEs and across proxy metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic narrow TopK SAEs, polysemantic dictionary atoms emerge because they lower distortion under a rate cap. Whether they win depends on raw co-occurrence probabilities of concepts, not on correlation. A toy SAE rotates from a near-monosemantic initialization to a polysemantic one.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latent polysemanticity is an optimal response to concept co-occurrence under rate and width constraints.

fits_no_version.finding: Most SAEBench interpretability proxies, including AutoInterp, fail the paper's RDP monotonicity criterion on Gemma SAEs. AutoInterp has V=0.886 and ρ=−0.68 on TopK, and V=0.993 on ReLU. Only Splitting and Sparse Probing weakly agree, and only on TopK.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Common SAE polysemanticity proxy metrics do not track the predicted rate-distortion-polysemanticity tradeoff.

record.problems: The strongest results rely on stylized assumptions including orthogonal concepts, binary/aligned atoms, and zero biases. Real-world proxy audit uses precomputed SAEBench outputs and cannot validate proxies against ground-truth polysemanticity; uncertainty estimates are not reported.

untested.parts: Transformer MLP neuron polysemanticity and its layer variation: not studied.
Whether network neurons are polysemantic because of superposition: not studied. The toy results concern SAE atoms only.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure: not studied. Toy SAEs are narrow, so capacity pressure is present.
Share of polysemantic neurons across architectures or activations: not measured.
Reinterpretation of canonical polysemantic neurons: not studied.
Neuron-level polysemanticity classification by activation range or explanation scoring: not studied.

missing.what: Contributions say proxies are evaluated on GPT-2 SAEs too, but no GPT-2 results appear in the text.
missing.locator: Section 1 Contributions (iii); Section 4 and Table 2 report Gemma only

record.verdict_notes: The record linked SAE-latent results to V3 and V7, but every version concerns neurons of trained models. Superposition appears only in related-work discussion. The toy results bear on SAE dictionaries, so all rows are reassigned to none and recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Vision classifiers and neuron responses to image inputs.
Polysemanticity of MLP neurons in transformer language models, including layer variation.
The paper studies synthetic sparse autoencoders, not trained network neurons, and does not establish that the mechanism explains neuron polysemanticity in general.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is no capacity pressure.
The study does not measure polysemantic-neuron shares or show that they can be lowered without a large performance loss; TopK/ReLU are used in an audit of proxy metrics.
Whether apparently mixed neuron responses share one underlying feature or related jobs.
The study compares SAE polysemanticity proxies, but does not examine activation ranges or test neuron-level polysemanticity classifications.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Toy SAE settings with constrained rate and co-occurring concepts
reader_labels.reason: Polysemantic solutions can improve reconstruction under rate constraints, and their advantage depends on co-occurrence probabilities; this supports a qualified, data-dependent account rather than testing superposition in trained neurons (r1–r4).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Compared SAE proxy metrics on TopK and ReLU Gemma SAEs
reader_labels.reason: Proxy results vary markedly: some are anti-aligned, several are near the random baseline, and only two show weak agreement on TopK Gemma; ReLU results are mostly anti-aligned (r5–r40).
